title: The Brahmana from Maharashtra
html:
A Devotee Without a Name

Among those who served Sri Chaitanya in Varanasi, the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” more than once speaks of a man whose name no source has preserved. Krishnadasa Kaviraja calls him simply “the brahmana from Maharashtra” — maharashtriya vipra, dvija or brahmana (Madhya 17.101; 19.253; 20.79; 25.7, 58, 153, 172, 210) — and twice merely “a brahmana” (Adi 7.52; Madhya 17.105). The biographies, too, call him only this, without a name.

He came from Maharashtra but lived permanently in Kashi: “I live in Varanasi all the time,” he says himself (Madhya 25.10). Nothing more is known of his worldly life. The sources name neither his family, nor the year and day of his appearance, nor when he left this world; nor are his days found in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math. All that we know of him is bound up with the Lord's two stays in Kashi — on the way to Vrindavana and on the way back; by our timeline these were the years 1514–1516, when the Lord was twenty-eight to thirty years old.1

Who he was, Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati have told best. In the “Amrita-pravaha- bhashya,” in his summary of Madhya 25, Bhaktivinoda writes that the brahmana from Maharashtra was a servant of Mahaprabhu and was filled with joy on hearing the Lord's glory. And in his “Anubhashya” Bhaktisiddhanta heads the account of his first meeting with the Lord: “A brahmana from Maharashtra comes and becomes a follower of the Lord” (on Madhya 17.101).

The First Meeting

The Lord first came to Varanasi on His way to Vrindavana. Tapana Mishra and Chandrashekhara gave Him shelter, and the devotees of Kashi, hearing of His arrival, came to bow at His feet; according to one of the biographies, the brahmana from Maharashtra came together with Chandrashekhara, and the Lord embraced Chandrashekhara and spoke of Krishna with them all. Kaviraja says of him:

“A brahmana from Maharashtra would come to see the Lord, and he marvelled at His beauty and His love.” (CC, Madhya 17.101)

All the brahmanas of Varanasi invited the Lord, but He declined every invitation: “Today I already have an invitation.” So He did day after day, wary of the company of the Mayavadi sannyasis (17.102–103). This was neither pride nor intolerance: the Lord, playing the part of an acharya, explains Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in his “Anubhashya,” avoided bad association with the Mayavadis and took His meals only with devotees. At the head of the sannyasis of Varanasi then stood Prakashananda Sarasvati, who taught Vedanta to a great many disciples. The brahmana, who had seen the Lord's conduct, went to him and began to tell him about the Lord: of His golden form, of arms reaching to His knees and eyes like lotuses, of how all the signs of a maha-bhagavata described in the “Bhagavatam” were manifest in Him, and how the name of Krishna never left His tongue (17.105–114).2 But Prakashananda answered with mockery and blasphemy, called the Lord a “sentimental sannyasi,” and told the brahmana not to go to Him any more (17.115–121). So Prakashananda spoke while the Lord's mercy had not yet touched him; what became of him afterwards is told in the article about him.

“Hearing this, the brahmana was deeply pained. Saying ‘Krishna! Krishna!’ he rose and left that place. His mind had been purified by seeing the Lord. Sorrowfully he came before Him and told Him everything. Hearing this, Mahaprabhu smiled slightly.” (CC, Madhya 17.122–124)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta begins this passage with the words: “The brahmana, whose heart had been purified by the Lord's darshan…” (on 17.123).

And the brahmana asked the Lord what had given him no peace:

“‘While speaking of Your faults he uttered Your name, saying “Chaitanya, Chaitanya” three times. But not once in those three times did the name of Krishna come to his lips. He takes Your name with contempt, and hearing it pains me. Please be kind and tell me the reason for this. When I see You, my mouth says “Krishna!” and “Hari!”’” (CC, Madhya 17.126–128)3

The Lord answered him:

“The Lord said, ‘The Mayavadis are offenders against Krishna. They incessantly say “Brahman,” “atma,” “chaitanya” (consciousness). Therefore the name of Krishna does not come to their lips. The name of Krishna and Krishna's own form are one and the same.’” (CC, Madhya 17.129–130)

The name, the form and Krishna Himself are one and wholly spiritual, the Lord went on, and so the name does not reveal itself to one who offends Krishna (17.131–143). And at the end He said: “I came to Kashi to sell My wares of emotion, but there is no buyer” (17.144). According to one of the biographies, the Lord then also forbade the brahmana to associate with the Mayavadis and so granted him His mercy.4

“Saying this, Gaurahari made that brahmana His own, and rising early the next morning He set out for Mathura.” (CC, Madhya 17.146)

The Bengali says sei vipre atma-sat kari' — “making that brahmana His own.” This is not the recruiting of a follower: the Lord took him among His own, as He takes His pure devotees — and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta heads the verse: “Having shown mercy to the brahmana, the Lord sets out for Mathura.” One of the biographies adds that the Lord intended to deliver Kashi by Krishna's mercy later, on the way back.

The Lord did not leave alone:

“Those three followed Him, but the Lord forbade them, and from some way along the road He sent all three back home. In separation from the Lord the three would meet together and sing of His qualities, maddened with love.” (CC, Madhya 17.147–148)

Kaviraja does not name the three, but the account makes clear that they were Tapana Mishra, Chandrashekhara and the brahmana from Maharashtra.5

In Kashi Again

After visiting Vrindavana, the Lord came to Varanasi again. He made Chandrashekhara's house His residence and took His meals with Tapana Mishra, not wishing to eat with the sannyasis (Madhya 19.251–252). And Kaviraja at once remembers our brahmana:

“A brahmana from Maharashtra came and met Him, and the Lord, out of affection, showed him His mercy.” (CC, Madhya 19.253)

“The brahmana from Maharashtra receives the Lord's mercy,” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta heads this verse. This time the Lord stayed in Kashi two months (Adi 7.47; Madhya 25.3), and for those who had come to love Him on His first visit it was as if life itself had returned: Tapana Mishra, Chandrashekhara, the brahmana from Maharashtra and others could once more serve Him in person, as one of the biographies also says.6

In those days Sanatana Gosvami came to Kashi from Bengal, and the Lord Himself brought him together with the brahmana:

“The Lord introduced Sanatana to a brahmana from Maharashtra, and that brahmana gave him a standing invitation: ‘Sanatana, as long as you stay in Kashi, please take your meals at my house.’ Sanatana said, ‘I shall live by madhukari, begging a little from house to house. Why should I take all my meals at one brahmana's house?’ The Lord was boundlessly pleased by Sanatana's renunciation.” (CC, Madhya 20.79–82)

In Bengali the brahmana offers Sanatana a maha-nimantrana, a “great invitation” for the whole time he is in Kashi; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta heads these verses accordingly: “Sanatana meets the brahmana from Maharashtra,” “The brahmana invites Sanatana to his house every day.” Sanatana, declining so ample an alms, chose madhukari — begging a little in many houses, as a bee gathers honey from many flowers — and this true renunciation (yukta-vairagya) delighted the Lord beyond measure. So the brahmana's hospitality became the occasion for showing the world Sanatana's renunciation.7

The Invitation

Meanwhile the sannyasis of Varanasi did not relent and blasphemed the Lord as before. The brahmana from Maharashtra could not hear it calmly. The “Charitamrita” tells what was in his heart:

“Everywhere the sannyasis blasphemed the Lord. Hearing this, a brahmana from Maharashtra reflected sorrowfully: ‘Whoever sees the Lord's nature at close hand perceives who He truly is and accepts Him as Ishvara, the Supreme Lord. If by some means I can bring them together, the sannyasis will see this and become His devotees. I live in Varanasi all the time. If I do not do this, I shall grieve for ever.’” (CC, Madhya 25.7–10)

“The brahmana from Maharashtra reflects with pain in his heart,” “The wish to bring everyone together” — so Srila Bhaktisiddhanta heads these verses. This was no scheme to “stage a debate,” and no trick. The brahmana's heart ached for the Lord's glory, and at the same time he wished the blasphemers themselves well: let them only see the Lord at close hand, he thought, and they will become His devotees. Bhaktivinoda Thakura, calling him a servant of Mahaprabhu, sees service in this care.

“Thinking thus, he invited all the sannyasis. Then that brahmana came to the place where Mahaprabhu was staying.” (CC, Madhya 25.11)

He came at the very moment when Chandrashekhara and Tapana Mishra, unable any longer to hear the Lord blasphemed, were pleading at His feet: “We cannot bear it; we would rather give up our lives” (Adi 7.49–51; Madhya 25.12). The Lord heard them with a slight smile, and then:

“Just then a brahmana came to meet Him. He came and, clasping the Lord's feet, made his petition: ‘I beg one thing of You; be pleased and grant it. I have invited all the sannyasis; if You come too, my heart's desire will be fulfilled. I know that You do not go to gatherings of sannyasis; yet be merciful to me and accept my invitation.’” (CC, Adi 7.52–55)

In the Adi-lila this brahmana is not named. But in the Madhya-lila Kaviraja tells of the same invitation again: the brahmana from Maharashtra (25.7) invited all the sannyasis and came to the place where the Lord was staying (25.11); “just then the brahmana came and invited Him. With great humility he clasped the Lord's feet” (25.14); the Lord accepted and the next day went to his house — and here the author refers directly to his earlier, detailed account (25.15–16). “A brahmana from Maharashtra comes and invites the Lord,” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta heads verse 25.14. Thus the brahmana who invited the Lord to the sannyasis and the brahmana from Maharashtra are one and the same person, and by the account of Madhya 17 he was also the one who had earlier heard Prakashananda's mockery.8

“Smiling, the Lord accepted the invitation; He made this gesture to show mercy to the sannyasis. The brahmana knew that the Lord does not go to anyone's house, but, inspired by the Lord Himself, he pressed Him with great insistence.” (CC, Adi 7.56–57)

Here is the key to the whole story. The wish to gather the sannyasis was placed in the brahmana's heart by the Lord Himself, for He Himself wished to show them mercy; the devotee's request became the instrument of His mercy. And the Lord, who had so far answered the blasphemers only with a smile, accepted the invitation not out of compliance and not for the sake of honour: one of the biographies calls His consent “only a gesture to save the sannyasis.”

“The next day the Lord went to the brahmana's house and saw the sannyasis all seated there.” (CC, Adi 7.58)

The Madhya-lila adds that the Lord came after His midday duties (25.15). “The Lord enters the assembly of sannyasis,” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta heads this verse. What followed is told in the article about Prakashananda: the Lord, showing the dharma of a Vaishnava sannyasi — amani-manada, seeking no honour for oneself and honouring others — sat down by the place where feet are washed and called Himself a sannyasi of a lower branch; His radiance drew the hearts of the sannyasis; Prakashananda himself called Him into the assembly; the Lord told them the instruction of His guru: “From the Krishna-mantra will come release from samsara, and by Krishna's name You will attain Krishna's feet” (7.73–74); and after the talk on Vedanta the sannyasis were changed and, begging forgiveness, cried out: “You are the Vedas embodied — Narayana Himself” (Adi 7.148); and the Lord forgave their offences and graced them with Krishna's name (7.150).9

The talk ended with a meal in the brahmana's house:

“Then all the sannyasis took their meal together with Mahaprabhu, seating Him in their midst. After the meal Mahaprabhu returned to His lodging.” (CC, Adi 7.151–152)

So in the house of the brahmana from Maharashtra the deliverance of the sannyasis of Kashi began. In Adi 7 Kaviraja describes it in detail, and in Madhya 25 only briefly, referring back to the earlier account: “I have described the Lord's mercy to the sannyasis before, in detail. Here I mention it again, briefly” (25.6; cf. 25.16–17).

Good News

The change in Prakashananda was real. Once, when his disciple was glorifying the Lord's teaching, Prakashananda himself supported him and said:

“‘The words of Sri Krishna Chaitanya are a stream of nectar. Whatever He declares is the truth, the very essence.’” (CC, Madhya 25.57)

The brahmana from Maharashtra was present and could not contain his joy:

“Hearing all this, the brahmana from Maharashtra happily went to tell the Lord.” (CC, Madhya 25.58)

“The brahmana from Maharashtra goes to give the Lord the good news,” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta heads this verse. He who had once left Prakashananda with pain in his heart now hurried to the Lord with news of the mercy the Lord had shown that very man. There is no gloating in him, no triumph over the defeated — only joy that one more soul had turned to the Lord.

“At that time Mahaprabhu, having bathed at Panchanada, was on His way to see Lord Bindu-madhava. On the way the brahmana told Him everything. Hearing it, Mahaprabhu smiled gently with pleasure.” (CC, Madhya 25.59–60)

According to one of the biographies, this was the Lord's daily custom in Kashi: having bathed at Panchanada, He would go to Bindu-madhava Hari. And the brahmana told Him all he had heard from the lips of Prakashananda, who had now become a devotee; “The Lord rejoices to hear from the brahmana from Maharashtra of Prakashananda, who has become a devotee,” writes Srila Bhaktisiddhanta on 25.60.10

At Bindu-madhava the Lord danced in kirtan, Prakashananda came there with his disciples, and a conversation on the “Bhagavatam” began between them. When it turned to the “atmarama” verse (SB 1.7.10), the brahmana again stepped forward:

“Just then the brahmana from Maharashtra told the assembly how the Lord had explained that verse: ‘The Lord has explained the meaning of this verse in sixty-one ways; all who hear it are amazed.’ Then everyone insisted on hearing them, and the Lord unfolded the sixty-one meanings in detail. Hearing them, the people were struck with wonder and concluded that Chaitanya Gosani is Sri Krishna Himself.” (CC, Madhya 25.153–156)

These sixty-one explanations the Lord had earlier given to Sanatana (Madhya 24). The brahmana wanted only one thing: that others too should see what he had seen. “The brahmana from Maharashtra praises the Lord, who can give sixty-one explanations,” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta heads verse 25.153.

The Farewell

For five days the Lord gave deliverance to all who came to Him, and on the sixth He left Varanasi:

“When the Lord rose at night and set off, five devotees followed close behind Him: Tapana Mishra, Raghunatha, the brahmana from Maharashtra, Chandrashekhara and Paramananda the kirtan singer — these were the five. All of them wished to go to Nilachala with the Lord, but He took leave of them all with loving care: ‘Whoever wishes may come later to see Me; now I shall go alone by the path through Jharikhanda.’” (CC, Madhya 25.171–174)

As on His first visit, the Lord sent those who followed Him home with love — but this time with the promise of meeting in Puri. Whether he went there afterwards, the sources do not say.

Soon afterwards Rupa Gosvami and his brother Anupama came to Varanasi.

“There Rupa met the three — the brahmana from Maharashtra, Chandrashekhara and Tapana Mishra.” (CC, Madhya 25.210)

Rupa stayed with Chandrashekhara, heard from Tapana Mishra the instructions the Lord had given Sanatana, and learned with joy how the Lord by His mercy had delivered the sannyasis of Varanasi (25.211–212); according to one of the biographies, Rupa heard all this from all three.11 This is the last the sources tell of the brahmana from Maharashtra.

As Others Tell It

Of the other original sources, only Govinda-deva in the “Gaura-krishnodaya” speaks of the invitation to the sannyasis: the sannyasis of the city disregarded the Lord, but one night, “at someone's invitation,” He came to them with a few companions (16.29). Who invited Him the poet does not say; we follow the “Charitamrita,” according to which the Lord came by day, on the day after the invitation, to the house of the brahmana from Maharashtra.12

His Significance

The brahmana from Maharashtra left behind no name, no writings, no disciples. Yet through him the Lord performed one of His most wonderful pastimes — the deliverance of the sannyasis of Kashi. He came every day to see the Lord, enchanted by His beauty and love; he could not bear the Lord to be blasphemed and, with Krishna's name on his lips, walked away from the blasphemer; he invited Sanatana to take his meals in his house; and, seeing that the sannyasis of Kashi went on offending the Lord, he wished them to see Him at close hand and invited them to his home. That wish, says the “Charitamrita,” was placed in his heart by the Lord Himself, for He wished to show the sannyasis mercy. Such is the way of mercy: the Lord acts through the heart of His devotee, and a servant's humble request becomes the gate of deliverance for many. And the brahmana himself remained what Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura called him — a servant of Mahaprabhu who rejoices in the Lord's glory and in the mercy poured out on others.

Notes

  1. The biographies and commentators give the years of the Lord's stays in Kashi differently: they convert the years of the Shaka era into our reckoning in different ways.
  2. Some translations render Madhya 17.105 “one of the brahmanas”; the Bengali has eka vipra, “a brahmana.” That this is the same brahmana from Maharashtra is clear from the account: he came to the Lord every day (17.101), told Him of Prakashananda's mockery (17.123–128), and the Lord “made that brahmana His own” (17.146). So too Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya,” and the biographies, understand it.
  3. One of the biographies retells this conversation differently: the brahmana himself supposedly spoke the Lord's name “Krishna Chaitanya” three times to Prakashananda, who said “chaitanya” three times but could not pronounce “Krishna”; and the brahmana supposedly begged the Lord: “Deliver this city of Kashi!” In the “Charitamrita” it is Prakashananda who says “Chaitanya” three times, the brahmana only asks the reason, and there is no such plea. We follow the “Charitamrita.”
  4. So writes Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya,” in his summary of Madhya 17. The verses themselves (17.129–146) contain no direct prohibition: the Lord explains why the name does not come to the Mayavadis and makes the brahmana His own — while it was Prakashananda, on the contrary, who told the brahmana not to go to the Lord (17.121). The prohibition, if understood so, is for the sake of the brahmana's own bhakti, not hostility to people.
  5. This is an inference from the context: Tapana Mishra and Chandrashekhara are named just before (17.82–100), and 17.146 speaks of “that brahmana.”
  6. One of the biographies writes that this time the Lord stayed in Kashi ten days. According to the “Charitamrita,” He spent ten days there on His first visit, on the way to Vrindavana (Madhya 17.100), and two months on the way back.
  7. One of the biographies says only that the brahmana invited Sanatana, without mentioning that the Lord introduced them; this is an omission, not a discrepancy.
  8. In the Bengali of Madhya 25.14 he is simply “the brahmana” (vipra; some translations add “that Maharashtrian brahmana”): who he is follows from 25.7–11. Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura and the biographies also see the brahmana from Maharashtra in the brahmana of Madhya 17. One of them tells of the brahmana from Maharashtra only the invitation and the events of Madhya 25, and his first meeting with the Lord elsewhere.
  9. One of the biographies, retelling this account, refers to verses 7.148 and 7.150 as “Adi 8” — a misprint; its other references are correct. It also cites the view of Shankara's school that only brahmanas who have taken sannyasa in one of its ten orders are true, “Vedic” sannyasis. This is the view of those sannyasis themselves. In calling Himself a sannyasi of a lower branch the Lord was not admitting any real inferiority but showing the humility of a Vaishnava sannyasi (“Anubhashya” on Adi 7.64); He is Bhagavan Himself, and the sannyasis themselves admitted: “You are Narayana Himself” (Adi 7.148).
  10. One of the biographies renders this passage in a compressed sentence from which one might understand that the news was brought by “a devotee of Prakashananda,” that is, his disciple. According to the “Charitamrita” and the “Anubhashya,” the brahmana from Maharashtra told the Lord the words of Prakashananda himself, who had now become a devotee. In general the biographies say less of the brahmana than the “Charitamrita” and follow here the “Anubhashya” and the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya”; we build the account on the “Charitamrita.”
  11. This biography also writes that Rupa stayed in Kashi two weeks; according to the “Charitamrita,” ten days (Madhya 25.214). And according to the “Charitamrita,” Rupa heard of the instructions to Sanatana from Tapana Mishra (25.211).
  12. The further account of the meeting with the sannyasis in the “Gaura-krishnodaya” also differs from the “Charitamrita”; it is discussed in the article on Prakashananda Sarasvati.
